conservation.condition_narrative:
Currently, all paints appear secure and stable, despite microscopic, intermittent, limited, and superficial cracking in the paints at the stretcher bar turn-down edges and isolated high warp threads. Despite the single key, the canvas remains moderately taut on the stretcher and has only planar deformations associated with the artist's original stretching. The matte, opaque zinc oxide white in the upper, viewer's left corner appears to have a modulation of opacity related to the thickness of the paint application and brushwork textures. 
 
 
 
The work formerly had a series of generalized small, spatter droplets of accreted white wall paint, as well as finger smudge soiling generalized across the edges. These were removed in the 2017 cleaning. Three prominent, bright white, pinpoint holidays are visible. There is a superficial horizontal abrasion/scuff with dark media in the lower viewer's right corner. There is a horizontal line of thinned paint, below the midpoint and just viewer-right of center, which is associated with four proud threads. This is not an abrasion but apparently part of the artist's technique. The work appears unvarnished, and there is little sign of aluminum stearate blanching in the dark paint layers.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a 1 x 1 plain-weave, processed-linen, commercially primed canvas with warps stretched in the vertical orientation over an "American Type", double-bevel-faced, miter-cut ended, mortise-and-tenon joined, keyable softwood, commercial stretcher bar, pre-cut to the whole inch, 1 ¾" wide x ¾" thick in 9" and 7" sized lengths. The canvas is stretched and tacked using blued steel tacks spaced evenly apart. One original key is extant and taped to the stretcher. The canvas has 32 warp threads per inch (tpi) and 39 weft threads per inch (tpi). 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The processed linen canvas has a commercially applied primer consisting of 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2) and ZnO in oil, characterized using x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV, 33 and 40kV, and 28.8, 18, and 3.8 µA under full vacuum. 
 
  
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied over charcoal/graphite line under-drawing in single layers, such that the texture of the primed canvas is generally visible through the paint, and the canvas or primer functions as a reflective design surface. The artist has prepared her higher-value whites and lighter colors to achieve a matte, slightly stiff, cream-like consistency, which is slightly thicker than background paints and retains brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. White paint appears extremely matte. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies and allowed to flow and level into the texture of the canvas. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the canvas, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted, primed canvas to be a visible detail in the composition, with graphite underdrawing residues sometimes visible. Colors in the painting have been characterized using x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV, 33 kV, and 40kV, and 28.8, 18, and 3.8 µA under full vacuum, as zinc oxide white, P/Ca bone black, Co-Fe-Pb-Cr violet, and Fe ochre-Cr tan. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The work appears to be unvarnished. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary, micro-environmentally buffered, and gasketed Ni/Al metal-leaf "clam shell" profile frame, a reproduction of Georgia O'Keeffe's original design, created by framer/artist George Of. The buffering media is ArtSorb sheet, buffered to 45% RH, contained with the Marvelseal-lined frame backing panel with a micro-chamber activated charcoal/zeolite clay embedded paper cover as the dust-proof barrier. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer, which has a Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

conservation.condition_narrative:
All paints and structures are secure and stable. Stretcher bar inside edge creases and raised creases from verso impacts from historic backing hand-holes can generally only be seen in raking and specular light along the viewer's left vertical stretcher. The edges of forms are often defined by raised linear brushwork at the margins of the forms. These sometimes fracture and flake as a result of canvas deflection/excursion in transit. There is an isolated, aggregated area of glossy varnish along the viewer's left vertical finger protrusions. These are of unknown origin. The work is clean and free of dust. All accretions have been previously removed. 
 
 
 
Brush-hairs, dried pallet bits, and other studio inclusions are occasionally visible in the design surface but should not be confused with damage or deterioration. The work has developed occasional, generalized distributions of very fine basic lead carbonate (2PbCO3-Pb(OH)2) micro­protrusions that appear under some magnification as small granular surface inclusions in the paints. They are also visible in the primed canvas along the tacking edge where there are no paints.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a 1 x 1, commercial, plain-weave, linen canvas stretched over an "American Type", double-bevel-faced, miter-cut ended, mortise-and-tenon joined, keyhole softwood, commercial stretcher bar, pre-cut to the whole inch, 1 ¾" wide x ¾" thick in 9" and 7" sized lengths. The canvas is stretched with the warps in the horizontal position and tacked using blued steel tacks spaced evenly apart, 1" to 1.5" with regularity. No keys are used in the stretcher. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The canvas has a commercially applied primer consisting of ZnO in the largest percentage and 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2 in oil, characterized using x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV and 40kV and 28.8 and 3.8 µA under full vacuum. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Graphite line underdrawing is occasionally visible at the margins of adjacent forms, but can be seen intermittently in transmitted light and in IR. The work is executed in single layers, generally wet-into-dry, using vehicular, cream-like paints. Brush texture is generally leveled with the fine texture of the canvas weave, which is generally visible in the darker values. Brighter value background forms are executed in more stiff, paste-like paints, which retain the texture of the brushwork. There are frequent linear raised ridges of paint at the margins of the forms. The artist's subtractive technique is seen in discrete areas where paint has been rubbed thin from the high-relief threads, exposing the primer below and lightening the value of the color. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting does not appear to be varnished overall. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in a reproduction, Georgia O'Keeffe/George Of-designed "clam shell" profile, aluminum/nickel leaf frame with gasketed, Optium non-reflective acrylic glazing and a gasket-sealed, secondary backing strainer which contains both conditioned silica gel felt and zeolite/charcoal embedded boards as a humidity buffer.

conservation.condition_narrative: The drawing is unfixed, complete, and retains all the original structural and material elements applied by the artist at the time of fabrication. The mounting is secure, and the mat and backing materials are stable. There are handling finger dents that are best seen in raking illumination, at either side and below the mid-point of the vertical dimension. There are repetitive cockles across the top and bottom edges, possibly as a result of the historic rolling of the sheet. There are numerous inclusions in the paper.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a sheet of medium-thick, cream-colored, slightly textured, Ingres-type laid paper. Chain lines move vertically across the composition. There is a watermark in the lower viewer's right corner in reverse that reads "MICHALLET (France)." 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** There is no visible sizing or fixative visible in normal or UV light, although dilute gelatin sizing would be difficult to see, even in UV. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Charcoal is applied with dense, curvelinear outlining and with various degrees of shading, fill, and overlap. There is no subtractive work visible. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** No fixative or surface coating is visible. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a 2006 white wash maple frame with secondary basswood backing and strainer. The over-matted 8-ply, cotton-finer Rising Museum mounting board (warm-white) window mat is folio taped to the 4-ply backing mat of the same type. The sandwich system of Optium tin-titanium optically coated acrylic is sealed to an acid-free, zeolite- and charcoal-embedded backing board. An insulating panel of acid-free Fome-Cor board is added to the back.

conservation.condition_narrative:
The work has been historically lined with wax-resin to a 2 x 2 linen canvas, similar to the original in weight. This canvas is one known to have been previously used and recommended by Caroline Keck. The lined work appears to have been stretched onto the original, 1 ¾" wide, ¾" thick, double-bevel faced "American Style" commercial stretcher, with new blued-steel tacks located in the original tacking holes. The stretcher currently has no keys in the corners. Tension is presently maintained by the attachment of the new microclimate backing strainer. 
 
 
 
The wax-resin lining appears to have slightly saturated and darkened the paints in thinly applied or slightly translucent regions in the white background passages. This translucency is also visible in the consolidated stretcher bar cracks above the inside edges of the stretcher bars in the white-painted background areas. Several vertically oriented weft threads and canvas slubs have been thrown slightly forward in relief as a result of the lining process. The design layers in those planar deformations appear stable. There is an old diagonal crack in the top center of the horseshoe form that appears to remain largely planar and well adhered. 
 
 
 
There are edge abrasions and edge losses resulting from frame abrasions and turn-down edge strains. Pb carboxylate soap microprotrusions are very small and generalized throughout the work. However, the population of soap protrusions is far denser in the umber and red ochre and gray regions of the foreground and is more isolated in the thicker white background paints. An interlayer crack appears in the transmitted infrared image in the viewer's right, near the horseshoe. This crack has not yet migrated to the surface of the painting and is not yet visible on the surface in normal observation.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The original support is a plain weave, 2 x 2, polished linen canvas, having approximately 30 warp and weft thread pairs per inch. Documentation suggests that conservator Caroline Keck likely executed the wax lining of this work on a secondary, 2 x 2 plain-weave canvas around 1958. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The raw canvas appears to have been given a very dilute protein sizing and was primed by the artist with a dilute single coat of commercial white pigment in oil, consisting exclusively of Zn, Ca, and S. That may have been followed by a heavy, bright, lead-white overall coating over the recto, but excluding the tacking edges. It is also possible that the heavy lead white coating overall is part of the design layer. A selvedge edge of the canvas is visible on the top tacking edge of the painting, with the warps oriented horizontally. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Graphite underdrawing is occasionally visible under magnification in areas where the paints of adjacent forms do not overlap, indicating that the general forms were underdrawn. Paints are generally applied in single, thin layers, often smoothed with a palette knife in the white background regions, with the canvas weave surface texture often visible. Brush textures remain part of the painterly effect in the foreground, feather, and reflection forms. The margins of forms often display raised, elongated ridges of a defining brushstroke. Paint pigments were characterized using the Bruker III-V XRF spectrometer at full vacuum, with settings of 15 kV, 4 μA, and 40 kV, 29 μA, respectively. The bright whites in the background were characterized as Zn and Pb whites. Foreground greenish gray was characterized as viridian Cr green blended with Zn. While a dark brown or red is suspected in the paint mix, there were no signals of Fe, Cd, or Hg. The bright feather tip whites were characterized and Pb with some Fe yellow ochre, the red streaks were Fe ochre red and yellow with Zn, and the blacks were characterized as bone black with P, Ca with traces of Fe. The horseshoe browns were characterized as Fe umbers, Cr viridian green, and Pb and Zn white. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The work appears to have a moderate, brush-applied synthetic varnish. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** Frame is a 1960s era painted and plated, Peter Bayle L-profile rolled brass frame with brushed chrome or nickel plating, with reinforced secondary frame backing and Optium acrylic glazing.

conservation.condition_narrative:
With the exception of some paint flake loss at the edges of the support (and paints on the verso as noted above in the section on ground/support preparation), all paints appear secure and stable. The support is in good plane overall. There are numerous scattered holidays in the paint layer as a result of the artist's compositional technique. These should not be mistaken for losses. There is a shallow, linear abrasion in the varnish across the lower left of the horseshoe, near the tip of the feather (near the black edge), and at isolated areas on the top and bottom edges. A loss at the mid-left edge of the support has resulted in a small associated crack in the paint at the left edge. Some of the white areas that the artist smoothed with a palette knife or similar suggest a darker color below. 
 
 
 
There are isolated accretions and inclusions. Basic lead carbonate micro-protrusion grains and micro-blisters (2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2) have begun to appear, primarily in areas (lower part of painting) containing green paint, but these are very difficult to see, even in strong raking light.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The work is executed on a laminated, composite cardboard panel. Small indentations at the board edges indicate the painting was likely previously installed in a frame using nails. Small bits of the paper structure are easily dislodged. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The priming on the recto appears to be basic lead carbonate in oil, as identified using XRF at 15 kV, 28.8 μA, and 40 kV, 3.8 μA, with full vacuum. There is a coating of titanium dioxide white magna color on the verso, applied in 1975 at the request of the artist. Below this coating, red, green, grey, and blue paint, likely oil-based, can be seen, and these paints have a tendency to shed small bits of paint. The priming appears to have been applied by the artist and is a white ground of lead carbonate in oil. The priming appears generally secure and stable and can be seen intermittently on the board edges. Flaking of the paper from the support and small colored paint bits from under the white coating on the verso tend to easily flake, while some bits appear to be stuck to the verso surface. The white acrylic coating has flaked, leaving the colored paints exposed at the edges. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Paints are generally thinly applied in single and double layers as creams and liquids, executing transitions in value or hue by painting wet–abutting dry. The artist has raised ridges of paint with her brushwork at the edges of many forms. Background whites were smoothed by the artist using a palette knife or a similar tool. Graphite underdrawing is occasionally visible at the edges of forms in both holidays between and under paint application. Small bumps/micro-protrusions are present (primarily in green or variations of green) on the surface and indicate the presence of soaps. Paints have been preliminarily characterized using X-ray fluorescence as basic lead carbonate and zinc oxide whites, bone black, burnt umber, red ochre, yellow ochre, and viridian chrome green, all in drying oil. 
 
  
 
**Surface Coating:** A yellowed and lightly soiled synthetic resin varnish, thickly brush-applied, is present overall. Treatment documentation suggests that the work was last varnished in 1975 using Acryloid B-67 iso- and n-butyl methacrylate copolymer. Localized consolidation of the fragmented panel edges was also executed at this time, as was the removal and overpainting of a painting on the verso, at the request of the artist. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is installed in a reproduction Georgia O'Keeffe III "clam shell" profile metal leaf, environmentally controlled frame with a gasketed secondary backing basswood strainer and gasketed Optium glazing.

conservation.condition_narrative: The work is planar with the exception of stretcher bar creases on the inside of the stretcher bar at the top, left, and right. The structure and media are secure and stable, and there are no readily apparent cracks, abrasions, or losses in the design surface. The dense areas of dark red-umber paint application exhibit spots of generalized opaque varnish separation at complex brush texture areas. There are frequent "holidays" in the artist's paint application, particularly at the margins and intersections of forms, resulting in spots and streaks of unpainted, primed canvas. These should not be confused with losses in the design layers. Under magnification, it is also possible to observe, in raking light, prominent micro-protrusions generalized across the work in the paint under the varnish. These are the result of soap development in the paint film from the primer and may result in periodic pinpoint losses.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a 1 x 1 twill-weave, processed, linen canvas stretched over an "American Type", double-bevel-faced, miter-cut ended, mortise-and-tenon joined, keyable softwood, commercial stretcher bar, pre-cut to the whole inch, 1 ¾" wide x ¾" thick in 20" and 24" sized lengths. The canvas is tacked using blued steel tacks spaced evenly apart. Eight thin wood keys are extant. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The commercial proprietary priming appears to have been mechanically applied over a protein (gelatin) sized canvas and is a white ground of lead carbonate in oil, possibly with zinc or calcium carbonate amendments. The priming appears generally secure and stable across the tacking edges. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied over charcoal/graphite line under-drawing in single and double layers, such that the texture of the primed canvas is visible through the paint, and the canvas or primer functions as a reflective surface. The artist has prepared her higher value whites and lighter colors so that they have a somewhat stiff, cream-like consistency, which is slightly thicker than background paints and holds brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies and allowed to flow and level into the texture of the canvas with very isolated wet-into-wet blending. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the canvas, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted, primed canvas to be a visible detail in the composition, with graphite underdrawing residues sometimes visible. 
 
  
 
**Surface Coating:** There is a thin, clear, clean synthetic resin varnish, brush-applied, overall. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary, micro-environmentally buffered, and gasketed metal-leaf "clam shell" profile frame, a reproduction of O'Keeffe's original design, created by framer/artist George Of. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer which has Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

conservation.condition_narrative: All paints appear secure and stable, with the exception of small edge losses. As the artist applied stiff, matte paints, spaces at edges or where one color abuts another, occasional "holidays" or areas of the board are visible. On the large leaf at the right edge, there is a small gouge, and near that is a small dent, but the surrounding paint appears stable. There are small edge losses, but overall, the paints on the surface are stable and secure. There are also frame abrasions along all four edges of the painting face where the work historically rested against the rabbet of O'Keeffe's original frame, and these are also normally expected in O'Keeffe's works from this period. Small bumps seen on the surface may be paint bit inclusions or may, in some cases, indicate the presence of lead soaps. Preliminary tests indicate little grime on the surface.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a composite wood fiber panel, textured on one side, smooth on the other. The artist has painted on the smooth side. The board appears to be stable and in good plane. There are minor edge losses due to previous framing. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** There is no indication that the artist added sizing to the board surface prior to painting. It also appears that no ground layer was applied, but rather, the artist painted in oils directly onto the bare board. Many areas of bare board are visible below the paint layers. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** There does not appear to be graphite underdrawing, though it may be entirely covered by the paint application. The artist has prepared her higher-value whites and lighter colors to achieve a slightly stiff, cream-like consistency. The background (off-white), in particular, has the appearance of being "troweled" on using a palette knife, giving a textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies, but are more paste-like, whereas lighter values have been applied. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the support, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of the unprimed board to be a visible detail in the composition. The sides of the board have also been painted in oil in some areas as a carryover from the design, while in other sections, they merely suggest the compositional colors without direct contact with the color adjacent in the design. Small bumps seen on the surface may be paint bit inclusions or may, in some cases, indicate the presence of lead soaps. 
 
   
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting appears to have no varnish coating. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary, micro-environmentally buffered, and gasketed metal-leaf "clam shell" profile frame, a reproduction of O'Keeffe's original design, created by framer/artist George Of. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer, which has a Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

conservation.condition_narrative:
All paints appear secure and stable, despite microscopic, intermittent, limited, and superficial cracking in the paints at the right stretcher bar edge lip. There are also frame abrasions and retouching along all the top turn-down edge of the painting face, where the work historically rested against the rabbet of O'Keeffe's original frame. The paints in these edges are also stable and secure. The work is now moderately taut, and all keys have been taped in place to prevent them from falling and becoming wedged against the canvas verso in transit. The varnish is lightly soiled overall and particularly soiled at the top, bottom, and side margins from historic handling with soiled fingers and hands. This soiling appears superficial and may not permanently discolor the matte and porous paints applied by the artist. 
 
 
 
The stretcher lip creases along the viewer's left edge are an inherent result of aging. While this deterioration can become worse with time, it does not necessarily imply damage from handling and transport. The surface of the work exhibits a generalized, densely dispersed distribution of fine, sand-grain-appearing micro-protrusions. These are the result of alkaline pigment metal salts (2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2 and ZnO) in the priming and paints reacting with carboxylic acids and esters during periods of cycling humidity levels. The blister-like, thin-skinned grains are advanced in this work. The space between the glazing and painting in the front of the frame should be carefully examined for pinpoint and larger paint flakes that may have been dislodged by developing micro-protrusions.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a 1 x 1 twill-weave, processed linen canvas stretched over an "American Type" double-bevel-faced, miter-cut, mortise-and-tenon-joined, keyable softwood commercial stretcher bar, pre-cut to the whole inch, 1 ¾" wide x ¾" thick, in 20" and 16" lengths. The canvas is stretched with the warps in a horizontal position and tacked using blue steel tacks spaced evenly apart, 2" to 3" apart with regularity. The canvas has 44 warp threads per inch and 50 weft (twill weave) threads per inch. Eight custom basswood keys are secured at the corners. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The processed linen canvas has a commercially applied primer consisting of 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2 and some CaCO3 in oil, characterized using x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV, 33 and 40kV, and 28.8, 18, and 3.8 µA under full vacuum from the verso. 
 
  
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied over charcoal/graphite line under-drawing in single layers, such that the texture of the primed canvas is visible through the paint, and the canvas or primer functions as a reflective surface. The artist has prepared her higher value whites and lighter colors so that they have a somewhat stiff, cream-like consistency, which is slightly thicker than background paints and holds brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies and allowed to flow and level into the texture of the canvas. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the canvas, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted, primed canvas to be a visible detail in the composition, with graphite underdrawing residues sometimes visible. The paints have been preliminarily characterized as iron red ochre, iron yellow ochre, lead white, and lead white and CaP bone black using X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV and 33kV and 28.8 and 3.8 µA under full vacuum from three sample locations for each color. In this case, it is clear by the relative lack of micro-protrusions in the bone-black at the viewer's left margin that the Pb soap degradation is accelerated by the presence of basic Pb carbonate in the paints. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting has a thin, somewhat glossy synthetic acrylic varnish, apparently an iso-butyl methacrylate. 
 
  
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in a reproduction Georgia O'Keeffe/George Of-designed "clam shell" profile, microenvironmental-controlled with Volara gasketing at the glazing and the backing, as well as silica gel-felted fabric in the backing panel, conditioned at 47% RH. The glazing is Optium, tin-optically coated, non-reflective acrylic.

One custom basswood key has been used to replace the missing key and is secured in place. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The processed linen canvas has a commercially applied primer consisting of roughly equal parts 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2) and ZnO in oil, characterized using x-ray fluorescence spectroscopy at 15kV, 33 and 40kV, and 28.8, 18, and 3.8 µA under full vacuum from the verso. 
 
  
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied over charcoal/graphite line underdrawing in single layers, such that the texture of the primed canvas is visible through the paint, and the canvas or primer functions as a reflective surface. The artist has prepared her higher value whites and lighter colors so that they have a slightly stiff, paste-like consistency, which holds brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies and allowed to flow and level into the texture of the canvas. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the canvas, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted, primed canvas to be a visible detail in the composition, with graphite underdrawing residues sometimes visible. The artist has used subtractive techniques to reduce paints across the sky passages of the composition. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting has a thin, slightly yellowed and soiled, synthetic acrylic varnish, apparently an iso-butyl methacrylate. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in a reproduction, Georgia O'Keeffe/George Of-designed micro-environmentally controlled frame.

conservation.technical_description:
The medium-weight, plain weave canvas is stretched onto a 4-member stretcher with “17” and “32” written on the stretcher verso. The canvas has been primed with a white priming layer which extends to the ends of the canvas. The canvas weave is strongly apparent through the thin paint and ground layers. Many skips in the paint reveal the ground below. 
The painting has an even, satin surface appearance. A label from the painting’s original backing board indicates that it was varnished with a synthetic resin in 1955. The varnish listed on the label is similar to that used by Caroline and Sheldon Keck to varnish many of O’Keeffe’s paintings, but the label does not directly attribute this work to them. 
The painting is framed in an artist’s original frame which was noted by Dr. Barbara Buhler Lynes to have been designed by Peter Bayle. The narrow metal frame is screwed into the sides of the canvas and has been painted to match the composition: it is primarily gray, but the sections of the frame where the painted waterfall touches it have been painted white (center of top and bottom frame members).

conservation.technical_description:
The work is executed with low impasto throughout; due to the sheer application of primer and paint, the darkness of the canvas is apparent. Several canvas imperfections are perceptible through the paint. Slubs are located as follows: one is 6 in. from the top and 6 in. from the right and ½ in. long.  Another is 13 in. from the top, 13 in. from the right edge and ¾ in. long.  A third is 7 ½ in. from the top, 2 ½ in. from the left edge and ½ in. long.  And the final slub is located 2 in. from the top, 6 ½ in. from the left and is 1 in. long.  Several spot imperfections are located in the lower left corner.  One is 2 in. from the bottom and 1 ¼ in. from the left.  Another is 4 in. form the bottom and 1 ¼ in. from the left.  A third is 11 ½ from the bottom edge and 6 ½ in. from the left. 
 
Several areas of the painting contain splatters of unknown origins. These areas are located in the upper right corner, around the center of the pink hollyhock, and below the center of the yellow hollyhock.

conservation.condition_narrative:
The painting was damaged and treated shortly after it was painted. Carolyn Keck was the conservator who treated it in 1955, and some of her treatment notes are written on the back of the panel. It was lined with wax-resin to linen before mounting to the panel. In addition, the painting was revarnished with B-72 in May of 2001 probably in preparation for sale to Gilcrease museum as indicated by a label stuck to the back of the painting. Winterthur library was contacted (where Keck treatment records are housed) but the librarian was unable to locate any records regarding treatment other than the painting belonged to a gallery at the time the treatment was done by Mrs. Keck. It is unclear why the painting was mounted to a panel. Cursory visual examination reveals a dent in the side of the antelope head and some inpainting there. 
 
DESCRIPTION: 
The painting shows an antelope skull floating in the sky. The flat-topped New Mexico mountain, Pedernal, is in the background. The frame appears to be original to the work and has been painted by the artist to continue the background onto the frame. 
 
CONDITION: 
Examination revealed a small flake of loose blue paint in the sky. The paint on the frame is grubby from handling. 
 
TREATMENT: 
The flake and a few other cracks in the blue sky were consolidated with Aquazol 200 in ethanol and water.

conservation.condition_narrative: The painting is unlined and appears unvarnished with a relatively matte surface. Two of the eight stretcher keys are missing and the corners are nailed closed. The canvas is slightly slack with a slight dip and buckling at the upper right. Debris between the stretcher bar and canvas is causing a curving bulge along the lower edge, right of center. There is a stretcher bar crack along the top. The tacking margins are taped and the work is housed in the artist's original silver-tone thin-profile metal frame.
conservation.report_notes: Information provided for *Access O'Keeffe* by Art Institute of Chicago in 2025.
conservation.technical_description: The painting is executed on a single piece of canvas tacked to a four-member keyable stretcher with standard size markings (20 and 36, respectively) imprinted on the bars. The work is thinly painted and the canvas texture remains visible throughout.

conservation.condition_narrative: The object is in good and stable condition. The object is a preparatory sketch for the painting Brooklyn Bridge (77.11), also in the museum's collection. Horizontal creases near the upper edge of the sheet may have been created when the sheet was attached to a drawing board or possibly the painting's masonite panel as a means to transfer the friable drawing media to the primed panel. A myriad of creases down the center vertical axis of the sheet may have been created by the artist if she folded the paper in half lengthwise, to transfer the design from one half of hte sheet to the other, for symmetry. Another possible theory is that the creases were created due to repetative folding the sheet to transfer the composition to the primed masonite panel. Horizontal creases throughout the sheet may have been created when the drawing was rolled in storage or may also be related to the artist's process. Two small punctures near each of the upper corners suggest the drawing was pinned to a surface. There are six strips of Japanese paper on the verso from a previous hinging campaign: two along the upper edge of the sheet, near the corners; two along the left edge; and two along the right edge. Abrasions and residual adhesive in two areas just above the center of the verso appear to have been created by tape, now removed.

other.content:
A photo of the verso shows an inscription on the stretcher bar. 
 
From Corcoran curatorial memo of 23 July 2007: 
“An inscription on the top stretcher bar in O'Keeffe's own hand reads "Emilia Oct - 48." 
Wondering whether this inscription might prompt us to reconsider the date of the painting, I contacted Barbara Lynes, author of the O'Keeffe catalogue raisonne. According to Lynes,"Emilia was a person who worked for O'Keeffe and probably helped her stretch canvases at various points in time." Lynes "suspect[s] that the stretcher was prepared then [1948]," but that "she returned to it in 1953, when she painted the picture."” 
 
Email from Barbara Lynes of 23 July 2008 confirms the inscription is in O’Keeffe’s hand (and that she had missed it when examining the painting for the CR). 
(Source: NGA, 2025)

cr_data.provenance:
(Doris Bry [1920-2014], New York).[1] (Noah Goldowsky Gallery, New York). Woodward Foundation, Washington, by 1966;[2] gift 1977 to the Corcoran Gallery of Art, Washington; acquired 2015 by the National Gallery of Art. (Source: NGA, 2025) 
 
[1] The first two owners are given in Barbara Buhler Lynes, _Georgie O'Keeffe: Catalogue Raisonné_, 2 vols., New Haven and London, 1999: 2:789, no. 1265. In a letter of 8 August 1953, the artist wrote to Edith Halpert that one of the four paintings she had sent that day to the Downtown Gallery was "Wall with Green Door/53" (Downtown Gallery Records, Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, cited in Lynes 1999). The painting was lent by Miss O'Keeffe through the Downtown Gallery to a 1960 exhibition of her work at the Worcester Art Museum, and there is a Downtown Gallery label on the reverse, on which the painting is given number 166. 
 
[2] The 1966 date is according to Lynes 1999, 2:789, no. 1265.

cr_data.provenance:
(Doris Bry [1920-2014], New York).[1] Susan and David Workman, New York.[2] (Kraushaar Galleries, New York). (Kennedy Galleries, New York, by 1977); private collection; gift 2021 to NGA. (Source: NGA, 2025)

[2] A label from the back of the painting names the couple as lenders to the 1970 retrospective exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art.
remarks_1999: Not recorded Whitney Archive. O'Keeffe wrote: "One morning the world was covered with snow. As I walked past the V of the red hills, I was startled to see them white. It was a beautiful early morning—black crows flying over the white. It became another painting—the snow–covered hills holding up the sky, a black bird flying, always there, always going away" (*Georgia O'Keeffe* [1976], unpaginated, text accompanying entry 86). (Source: Lynes, 1999)

conservation.condition_narrative: All paints appear secure and stable, despite microscopic, intermittent, limited, and superficial cracking in the paints at the stretcher bar creases. As the artist applied stiff, matte paints, the canvas was deflected into the stretcher bars, resulting in microscopic fissures and creases in the canvas and priming layers. Over time, these fissures further evolved into intermittent, hairline cracks through the paint and as raised creases on the surface. There are also frame abrasions along all four edges of the painting face where the work historically rested against the rabbet of O'Keeffe's original frame, and these are also normally expected in O'Keeffe's works from this period. The paints in these edges are generally stable and secure, though there is some minor paint loss at the upper edge. A scratch that is approximately 1 ½" in length is visible at the upper left in the blue sky area near the branch tip that crosses the white cloud. There is a small gouge at the lower right. The work is now moderately taut. The paints are lightly soiled overall and particularly soiled at the top, bottom, and side margins from historic handling with soiled fingers and hands. There are a few surface abrasions visible in ultraviolet light. Also visible in ultraviolet light are two small, discrete areas of previous retouching at the right edge, between the two green bushes, and just above that, at the far right edge.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a medium-weight, relatively open, coarsely-spun, basket weave, 2 x 2 linen or linen-jute blend over a typical, "American Style" double-bevel-faced, mortise-and-tenon, mitered-corner wood stretcher from Anco. Vertical and horizontal cross braces are in place with keys added and secured to those braces in 2007. There are also cardboard corner braces, tacked down, at each corner of the stretcher. The canvas exhibits minor cusping along the edges where the fabric was tacked to the stretcher. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The artist or her assistant appears to have applied a dilute protein size, such as rabbit-skin glue or gelatin, followed by a priming of alternating layers of lead carbonate (PbCO3) in oil and zinc oxide (ZnO) in oil. UV-auto fluorescence photography suggests that the artist applied a priming of commercial basic lead carbonate 2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2 in oil and a commercial zinc oxide (ZnO) and barium sulfate, BaSO4, in oil. The priming appears to be applied in limited coats without sanding. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Graphite underdrawing is only occasionally visible at the margins of adjacent forms. The work is executed in single and double layers of stiff, paste-like paints, with multiple layers used at the brightest values. Overall, the paint application is fairly dry, leaving many areas of holidays visible. These should not be interpreted as losses, and this technique is common to the artist. Brush texture is generally retained in the stiff paints of brighter values. Cream, vehicular paints, nearly smooth and leveled, occur primarily in the darker values. There are frequent, linear, raised ridges of paint at the margins of forms. Scrubbing or zigzag brushwork has often been used in brighter values. The artist has executed gradual, stepped transitions in value or hue. In ultraviolet light, a bright, whitish-green fluorescence is visible on both the right and left edges, where the sky meets the mountain form, indicating the presence of zinc in the paint. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** An n-butyl isobutyl methacrylate copolymer resin was spray applied to the painting in a 1955 treatment. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary, micro-environmentally buffered, and gasketed metal-leaf "clam shell" profile frame, a reproduction of Georgia O'Keeffe's original design, created by herself and the framer/artist George Of. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer which has Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

remarks_1999: Not recorded Whitney Archive. O'Keeffe wrote: "I have a small piece of an Antelope Head.. . that I like very much" (O'Keeffe to Edith Halpert, 8 August 1954, Archive of American Art). "We should have his [Mr. Marcus] picture [for 1954 exhibition] if we can get it — it is so different than other things and I think one of the best" (O'Keeffe to Edith Halpert, 26 February 1955, Archive of American Art). "Someone gave me a very fine antelope head with horns. It was supposed to be the old buck's head that had been shot.... There were many drawings and paintings of the antelope. Our antelope had horns that turned back with a short forward prong. But I also had horns that turned in" (*Some Memories of Drawings* [1988], unpaginated). (Source: Lynes, 1999)

conservation.condition_narrative: There are numerous generalized holidays in the artist's technique at the margins between forms, where brushstrokes do not meet, and the primed canvas is visible. There is a very slight, barely visible stretcher bar crease in the center left vertical with no cracks. There are stable, vertical, hairline cracks at the tacking edge on the left and right margins of the work, as indicated. There are two pinpoint, dry accretions visible in the lower left and right corners, as well as one accretion in the upper right corner. There is a loose fiber on the interior of the glazing in the lower left corner that casts a shadow in direct lighting. There are artist's media transfers across the lower edge. There are finger smudges on the tacking edges and the top of the mountain form.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a commercially primed linen with additional lead/zinc priming by the artist. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The processed linen canvas has an artist-applied primer, apparently consisting of roughly equal parts 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2 and ZnO in oil. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Thinly applied matte and gloss creams with ridges of paint often at the edges of forms. Holidays in the artist's application of paint occur frequently at the margins of forms. Work also has isolated areas of subtractive work by the artist. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting appears to be unvarnished. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in a reproduction, Georgia O'Keeffe/George Of-designed micro-environmentally controlled "clam shell" profile frame.

remarks_1999: Not recorded Whitney Archive, Downtown Gallery Archive, Abiquiú Notebooks. O'Keeffe wrote: "I live on a hilltop in a village.... From my eastern window the road out into the world seems to wind away far up and down. Nearby it seems to swoop under the house—then curves to the left instead and goes past me. The road winds along the foot of the hills at the edge of the mountains. A long dark mesa to the east—a ragged pink one to the west — a valley into the mountains to the south, then hills and a mountain to the north.... One day, playing with a camera, I tried to photograph the road and to get it all in I had to turn the camera at a very odd angle. My drawing—or painting—call it what you will—comes from that photograph" (*Some Memories of Drawings* [1988], unpaginated). (Source: Lynes, 1999)

conservation.technical_description:
Surface: The surface has intermittent small accretions and fibrous debris throughout. There are a few hairline cracks ranging from about 1/2" to 1 1/2" in length along the far outer edges of the surface at the upper center, upper right and lower left. The surface has a couple areas very minor loss at the upper right in the blue sky portion. There is a series of intermittent abrasions running along the far outer edge at the upper left of the surface. 
 
Frame: The frame shows signs of wear throughout with minor cracks and scratches, loss of gilding, minor nicks, abrasions and accretions. At the upper right corner is a single long 6 3/8" horizontal crack that continues inward towards the center of the frame.

conservation.condition_narrative:
All of the paints and the structure are secure and stable. The work is generally planar with no distortions and only stretcher lip strains along the turn-down edges of the canvas. The paints are free of cracks and other disruptions. All accretions have been previously removed. 
 
 
 
There are no visible abrasions in the design surface. There are no discolorations. There work is clean and free of dust. Brush-hairs, dried pallet bits, and other studio inclusions are occasionally visible in the design surface but should not be confused with damage or deterioration. 
 
 
 
The work has developed a broad, generalized distribution of basic lead carbonate (2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2) micro-protrusions that appear under some magnification as small granular surface inclusions in the paints. They are visible in the primed canvas along the tacking edge where there are no paints. They are more numerous and larger in the yellow ocher paints in this work.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a processed linen, 2 x 2 basket weave canvas stretched over a replacement, Lebron-type, expansion-bolt wood stretcher. The original tacks were replaced with steel staples when the work was re-stretched over a square, expansion strainer. It is clear from the application of both primer and paints that the original stretcher was largely out of square. This is likely the reason for the restretching sometime, probably before the 1970 transfer back to the artist from her agent, Doris Bry. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The canvas was prepared by the artist, possibly with the help of a studio assistant. The canvas appears to have been sized with a dilute rabbit-skin glue or other protein-based size, followed by alternating layers of basic lead carbonate in oil and zinc oxide in oil, without sanding. These priming materials were characterized using XRF at 15kV and 40kV at 4ua and 28ua, respectively. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied generally in single layers over occasionally visible charcoal/graphite line under-drawing, such that the surface of the canvas is a strong visible characteristic of the design surface. The artist has prepared her higher value whites and lighter colors so that they have a slightly stiff, cream-like consistency, which is slightly thicker than the darker values and occasionally holds more of the brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more liquid consistencies. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the design surface, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted primed canvas between the forms. The artist has utilized subtractive techniques such as scraping, rubbing, and blotting to thin paints in isolated areas. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting has a thin, apparently natural resin varnish with a strong yellow overall-induced auto fluorescence. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in an L-profile, off-white, powder-coated, extruded aluminum reproduction frame with microclimate provisions, including charcoal-zeolite embedded papers as VOC scavengers and conditioned silica gel-embedded felts for internal humidity control and buffering.

conservation.condition_narrative: All paints and the structure are secure and stable. The work has a crease and associated diagonal crack in the viewer's lower-right corner, which are stable and secure. All accretions have been previously removed. There are numerous abrasions and surface disruptions that likely occurred in the studio or in the artist's storage area, as they generally appear as if they occurred either in the artist's original wet paint or in wet or tacky varnish. There are no discolorations. The work is clean and free of dust. Artist's brush-hairs, dried palette bits, and other studio inclusions are occasionally visible in the design surface but should not be confused with damage or deterioration. The work has developed a broad, generalized distribution of basic lead carbonate (2PbCO3·Pb(OH)2) micro-protrusions that appear under some magnification as small granular surface inclusions in the paints. They are visible in the primed canvas along the tacking edge where there are no paints. They are more numerous and larger in thick paints, becoming very small in areas where the artist has removed paint using subtractive techniques during the execution of the work.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is processed linen, 2 x 2 basket-weave canvas stretched over a replacement, turn-buckle, expansion wood stretcher. The original tacks were replaced and augmented when the work was re-stretched over the expansion strainer. According to historic conservation records, the work was possibly re-stretched in 1961. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The canvas was prepared by the artist, possibly with the help of a studio assistant. The canvas appears to have been sized with a dilute rabbit-skin glue or other protein-based size, followed by alternating layers of basic lead carbonate in oil and zinc oxide in oil, without sanding. These priming materials were characterized using XRF at 15kV and 40kV at 4ua and 28ua, respectively. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied generally in single layers, often applied wet-into-wet and blended, filling the canvas texture. The artist also uses subtractive techniques such as scraping and wiping to remove paint and expose the white ground layer and canvas texture below, effectively creating a higher value. O'Keeffe applied paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the design surface, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted primed canvas between the forms. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting features a thin, glossy synthetic varnish that remains clear and clean. This varnish may have also been part of the 1961 conservation campaign. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The painting is installed in an L-profile, rub-out, powder-coated, extruded aluminum reproduction of Georgia O'Keeffe's original "L" profile brushed chrome frame. The frame is fitted with microclimate provisions, including charcoal-embedded zeolite papers as VOC scavengers and conditioned silica gel-embedded felts for internal humidity control and buffering.

conservation.condition_narrative: All paints appear secure and stable. There are frame abrasions along all four edges of the painting face where the work historically rested against the rabbet of Georgia O'Keeffe's original frame, and these are also normally expected in O'Keeffe's works from this period. The paints in these edges are also stable and secure. The work is planar and taut, but there is a very slight stretcher bar crease on the inside edge of the top stretcher bar, to the viewer's right of center. There are isolated insect accretions on the surface, but these appear to be easily removed. There are many holidays at the margins between forms where paints do not overlap and the primed canvas is visible; these should not be mistaken for losses or deterioration. There are isolated, pinpoint losses at the interstices of the weave, and these may be the result of transit vibrations. They are characterized by their sharp, fractured edges at the margins of the loss. One portion of the artist's typical linear, raised ridges of paint at the edges of forms has cleaved and is lost near the upper viewer's left corner. These ridges should be examined across the entire work after each transit to determine if there are other losses as a result of kinetic energy inputs.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a 2 x 2, bleached linen, closed, basket-weave with vertical warp thread orientation. The canvas was stretched over a 2 ½" wide, mortise-and-tenon, miter-corner, hardwood stretcher with large cardboard triangles nailed to each of the four corners to keep the stretcher taut and square. There are no stretcher crossbars. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The processed linen canvas has an artist-applied white primer appearing similar to that of roughly equal parts 2PbCO3•Pb(OH)2 and ZnO in oil. The primer was applied over a sizing of rabbit-skin glue, which appears thickly applied in isolated areas. Thin, graphite underdrawing is frequently visible at the unpainted margins between the forms. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** The paints have been applied over charcoal/graphite line under-drawing in single layers, such that the texture of the primed canvas is visible through the paint, and the canvas or primer functions as a reflective surface. The artist has prepared her higher-value whites and lighter colors to have a slightly stiff consistency, which retains brush texture as a compositional and textural effect. Darker values, by contrast, were prepared with more fluid, cream consistencies and allowed to flow and level into the texture of the canvas. O'Keeffe applies paint at the margins of forms using nearly continuous, curvilinear brush strokes with the brush positioned at a low angle to the canvas, resulting in a continuous, raised ridge of paint at the edge of each form. Surrounding brushwork is generally parallel to the linear directions defined by these edges, with no underlying or subsequent brushwork moving perpendicular to the linear form. Occasionally, adjacent forms do not overlap, and the artist has chosen to allow a "holiday" of unpainted, primed canvas to be a visible detail in the composition, with graphite underdrawing residues sometimes visible. The artist has also used subtractive techniques to thin paint and allow the white-primed canvas below to take on a more prominent visual character. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** The painting has a thin, slightly yellowed and soiled, synthetic acrylic varnish, apparently an isobutyl methacrylate. 
 
 
 
**XRF:** Primer stretched and primed by Georgia O'Keeffe. 
 
Right edge: lead carbonate, zinc oxide, tiny bit of calcium, tiny bit of titanium. 
 
Lower right corner, intense green: viridian green, barium, cadmium yellow, lead carbonate, zinc oxide. 
 
Middle left side, violet/purple: Cobalt, zinc, arsenic (Cobalt arsenate). 
 
Lower left side, pink: Cobalt, zinc. 
 
Bottom edge, center, blue: Cobalt, no iron, no silica, viridian green, tiny bit of cadmium (yellow). 
 
Center, dark green: cadmium (yellow), lead, sulfur, barium white, iron Prussian blue, zinc white, no chrome, no cobalt. 
 
Right side, between 2 pink vertical lines: zinc, synthetic alizarin. 
 
Soaps: Very few, very small, most numerous in viridian green. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary reproduction of an original Georgia O'Keeffe/George Of-designed Metalleaf, "clam shell" profile frame. The frame interior is fitted with Artsorb felt and Microchamber boards that buffer the interior conditions around a 45% RH setpoint and absorb acidic and oxidative VOCs generated by the original materials. The verso and recto are individually gasketed to form sealed air volumes on both sides, damping vibration and canvas displacement from transport and handling. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer which has Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

conservation.condition_narrative:
Cracks are present along the stretcher bar lip along all edges of the painting and intermittently around the inner edge of the stretcher bar. There is a curvilinear, branched crack near the top edge of the canvas to the left of the rock form. Numerous paint, brush, hair, or fiber inclusions are scattered throughout the painting. At the lower portion of the white area in the rock is a very thinly painted area, approximately ¼" in size. 
 
 
 
The upper left corner tacking edge was previously opened up, exposing cracks in the paint layer and frayed canvas fibers. This area was treated in 2011 using a Japanese paper hinge to stabilize the area. A small indentation, due to technique, may be seen in the brown paint near the top right side. There are small losses at the lower left and lower right corners. A few pinpoint losses may be found along the stretcher bar lip cracks. Abrasions from previous framing are visible at the top edge and on the upper left and right edges. There is a light abrasion at the center top edge and at the lower edge at approximately 3 ½" in from the left and ¾" up from the bottom. There is a very slight cusp at the lower right corner. Soiling is visible in the yellow area below the rock, right of center.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a medium-weight, relatively open, coarsely spun, basket-weave 2 x 2 cotton tacked to a commercial turnbuckle stretcher with metal corner inserts (stamped on stretcher). Canvas folds approximately ½" over to the back side of the stretcher and is tacked down, indicating preparation of the canvas by a studio assistant. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** Artist or artist's assistant appears to have applied a dilute protein size, such as rabbit-skin glue or gelatin, followed by a priming of alternating layers of lead carbonate (PbCO3) in oil and zinc oxide (ZnO) in oil. The priming appears to be applied in limited coats without sanding. X-ray fluorescence may reveal if barium sulfate is also present in the ground layer. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Graphite underdrawing is seldom visible at the margins of adjacent forms. The work is executed in single and double layers of stiff, paste-like paints, with multiple layers used at the brightest values. Brush texture is generally retained in the stiff paints of brighter values. Cream, vehicular paints, nearly smooth and leveled, occur only in isolated, dark values. There are frequent, linear, raised ridges of paint at the margins of forms. Scrubbing or zigzag brushwork has often been used in brighter values. The artist has executed gradual, stepped transitions in value or hue, often painting wet into dry in brief, slightly overlapping bands in a technique suggestive of pastel application. Brush strokes with grooves are evident in the fluid areas. There are raised brush edges where the black rock abuts the white background. Long fluid linear strokes create the base form on which the rock rests, and below that, short, dry, thin, and pasty paint application defines the side of the base form. The artist changes the background color from light green to white, presumably from 1963 to 1971, resulting in the thick appearance of the matte white background. This change also resulted in small flecks of green paint being transferred to other areas, likely through the use of the same brush. There is a small loose paint chip, appearing blue, white, and fibrous, at the bottom inside edge of the frame that is most likely from the tacking edge. Other, much smaller flakes are also seen along the bottom spacer. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** There are no records indicating a varnish application, though the surface slightly repels liquids. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary, micro-environmentally buffered, and gasketed, metal leaf "clam shell" profile frame that is a reproduction of Georgia O'Keeffe's original design, created by herself and framer/artist George Of. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer which has Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

conservation.condition_narrative: The canvas is in good plane and tension. There are losses and abrasions along the edges due to direct contact under the historic frames. There is a 4" long scratch (through the varnish) near the bottom of the painting. Another scratch (approximately 1 ½" long), through the paint layer, is located on the right side at 22 ¼" up from the bottom edge. There is a sideways "V"-shape burnish/scrape at the upper right quadrant. All dark brown passages in this area exhibit a mottled, spotty blanching in specular illumination. There are frequent and consistent holidays in the brushwork at the edges of painted forms; these are not damage.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is a medium-weight, relatively open, coarsely spun, basket-weave linen canvas over a typical, "American Style" double-bevel-faced, mortise-and-tenon, mitered-corner wood stretcher. All keys (new) are extant and secured for travel. Canvas has been trimmed flush with the verso of the tacking edges. The warps are oriented horizontally. 
 
 
 
**Ground or Support Preparation:** The artist or her assistant appears to have applied a dilute protein size, such as rabbit-skin glue or gelatin, followed by a priming of alternating layers of lead carbonate (PbCO3) in oil and zinc oxide (ZnO) in oil. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Graphite underdrawing is seldom visible at the margins of adjacent forms. The work is executed in single and double layers of thin, cream-like paints, which have generally leveled to reveal the full texture of the canvas. Brush texture is generally slightly retained in the liquid-to-slightly stiff paints of darker values. There are frequent, linear, raised ridges of paint at the margins of forms. There are often holidays, where the ground of the canvas is visible below, at the margins of forms where one color meets another. Scrubbing or zigzag brushwork has often been used in brighter values. The artist has executed gradual, stepped transitions in value or hue, often painting wet into dry in brief, slightly overlapping bands in a technique suggestive of pastel application. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** An isobutyl methacrylate resin varnish typical for the artist is suspected. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** The work is framed in a contemporary micro-environmentally buffered and gasketed, reproduction "L" profile rolled metal frame with brushed steel and lacquered finish with Optium acrylic glazing and new insulated secondary laminated basswood backing strainer that is a reproduction of Georgia O'Keeffe's original design with her post-1954 framer Peter Bayle. The glazing is Optium® tin salt-coated, UV-absorbing, static-free, non-reflective acrylic. The Optium glazing has a Volara closed-cell polyethylene gasket/pad. The frame is fitted with a laminated, Volara-gasketed backing strainer, which has a Security mirror-hanger and T-bolt hardware as well as D-rings.

remarks_post_1999: The painting features sandstone hues swirling around a patch of bright pink sky and is part of a series of paintings she completed in Glen Canyon. O’Keeffe often claimed that a good abstract work could be orientated as either a horizontal or vertical. In her records, “The Abiquiú Notebooks,” which include black and white photographs of each work, she or one of her assistants under her instruction often wrote “top” and “bottom” on the verso of these images. *On the River I* was oriented as a horizontal in her records and thus according to her preference in the Lynes publication. Examination of the work by the Museum’s Head of Conservation, Dale Kronkright, shows handing hardware on all stretcher bars. which occurs on many works, especially those completed late in her career. It suggests that the work may have once been oriented as a vertical. It is orientated in both ways in *Access O’Keeffe* to accommodate O’Keeffe’s preference as well as that she once may have thought of it as a vertical, thus proving her point that a good abstract work can be oriented as either a vertical or horizontal. (Source: O'Keeffe Museum, 2026)

conservation.condition_narrative: The work is generally planar, though it is very slightly cockled at the edges. The window mat is offset away from the work slightly to allow for the broad, slight, overall bow of the work. All media is securely attached, and there are no discolorations, holes, tears, or losses. There is a slight tape disturbance of the paper surface in the upper right corner. There are tiny, very isolated, black, pinpoint inclusions in the paper throughout. Paints have very sharply defined edges without liquid diffusion and are secure and stable. There are occasional, isolated, pinpoint transfers of blue watercolor. The work is hinged with wide Japanese mulberry fiber papers and methyl cellulose at three areas across the top edge and one each at the lower left and right corners of the bottom edge.
conservation.technical_description:
**Support:** The support is very thick, white, rough-textured, wove paper. Watermarks are visible in the upper left and lower right corners, reading "VERITABLE PAPIER D'ACHES TORCHON [sic]." 
 
 
 
**Ground:** None. 
 
 
 
**Design Layers:** Large, wide watercolor brushwork, slightly overlapped, in minimal application of paint with strict control over paint density or value. Brushwork creates spatial relationships of simplified linear or geometric forms with no underdrawing. 
 
 
 
**Surface Coating:** No coating is discernible over the painting. Paper support may have been sized by the artist prior to painting to diminish absorption into the surface. This is occasionally suggested by the stiff overall hand, broad cockling, and odd absorption dullness of UV auto-fluorescence. 
 
 
 
**Framing, Backing, and Hanging Hardware:** New white-wash-finish maple with Optium optical titanium-coated, non-reflective, anti-static acrylic glazing. Work has 100% cotton rag, buffered Rising Museum Mounting backing, and window mats. Frame has basswood secondary backing, strainer, and acid-free Fome-Cor backing with "T-bolt" security hardware. The work is "cradled" on the verso with an oversized sheet of Mulberry-fiber paper, which is trimmed and folded to form an enclosed border around the margins of the work. The Mulberry-fiber paper is then mounted to the backing mat. No adhesive is used on the work of art.
